utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we start, Mr. Ackerman, you don't mind Ms. Anneka behind?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So could you call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Julian Nicholls, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you all. Again, the same question, you don't mind that you have a member of my staff behind you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We don't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to make sure of that. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with David Cunningham and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Welcome back. I hope you have had some spare time, too, in which you could relax following the good work and the amount of work that you put in preparing the briefs for which I thank you on behalf of myself and Judge Janu and Judge Taya. We have gone through them, of course. We are also aware of the Defence motion to strike the Prosecution final brief. Yes, I recognise Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should add it was filed confidentially, I assume, because it refers to various confidential aspects of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say, I find myself in a slightly extraordinary position this morning, for two reasons: First of all, in the middle of my closing address, if Your Honours are going to say I should start this morning, there may well be a dramatic change in the law given that the judgement in the case of Krstic is going to be given, I understand at 11.00 this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that's the first aspect. The second aspect is that Your Honours have received, as Your Honour has just mentioned, a document that calls itself a motion which, if granted, would mean that our brief is null and void, and therefore the preparation for my speech, closing address, on which I have obviously relied heavily on what has already been said may be completely misguided and wrong. Your Honour, that is the unfortunate situation that has arisen since quarter to 6.00 last Friday when we received that document. Your Honour, we have with some reluctance in the light of its content have crafted a written reply to it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't seen that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We will file that today. However, as I say, Your Honour, it is a slightly odd situation because if Your Honours were minded to accede to this application, then my closing address would be probably completely different, and certainly a lot longer and a lot fuller. I don't know if there's anything that Your Honours want to say about that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll hear what Mr. Ackerman has to say first, and then we'll tell you what our idea is. Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we said fairly clearly in our written motion to strike the Prosecution's brief what it is we needed to say to Your Honours about it. I do want you to know that it was not filed lightly. It was something that received a great deal of consideration and a great deal of thought before deciding to file that motion because it is an unusual motion to file in a situation such as this. But we finally made the decision to do it, Your Honour, for this reason: This is not a justice of the peace court in some small town in Arizona. This is the International Criminal Tribunal. This is an international court that is trying to set itself up as a model for other courts around this world. And for the Prosecution to file a brief such as the one that was filed in this case, in my mind, is an insult to this Tribunal and a total disgrace. That's why we took the position that we took. It is absolutely riddled with factual errors. 11 people worked on that brief, Your Honour. We had three. That points up, among other things, the total disregard of equality of arms in this Tribunal. But they had 11 people working on it. They had plenty of time to check the footnotes, to see if they were accurate. And we pointed out some of the inaccuracies. I don't think we caught them all. We showed you some of them, and some of them are egregious to an extreme, and I can't imagine that they were mistakes. And that's why we filed the motion, and that's why we believe it should be taken seriously. And beyond that, what I have said in the motion is what we need to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are both aware that we do not take anything that you say orally or in writing for granted, and that if there are footnotes, we do check each and every one before we actually take stock of what the submission really amounts to. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's absolutely right, and that's, in effect, one of the matters that we will be raising in our written reply. Your Honour, I didn't want to dignify this motion with any oral response. I raised it because, as I say, the situation that now arises, that's the real problem in this case. Your Honour, we utterly, utterly refute any suggestion that the errors which occurred in the footnoting were done deliberately. Your Honour will have seen in the brief that we have actually in an attempt to assist as much as possible and to a far greater extent than that in the Defence brief, we have cited 1.702 footnotes, and wherever possible, we've actually given the page numbers, for the very reason that although we try to do our best to make sure that all citations are accurate, we know that errors can occur and we accept errors did occur. But they're there so that any assertions of fact made can be checked to see whether they are based in fact. And it is absolutely typical of the whole of the conduct of the Defence throughout this case that instead of simply accepting that errors can occur, it is immediately turned into an allegation of misconduct by the Prosecution. And it is a depressing thought that on the very last couple of days, that that pretense, because that's all it is, should be continued. Your Honours, as I say, the only difficulty is, and I leave it in Your Honours' hands as to how it should be dealt with, I'm put in a position where were Your Honours to accede to the motion, and I very much hope that Your Honours will treat it with the contempt that we say it deserves, my final address would be very different. And that's the real problem in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, -- yes, Mr. Ackerman, do you want to respond to that before we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, only to say this: Just as an example, to repeat in this brief that Tadeusz Mazowiecki visited Manjaca in the company of members of the ARK crisis staff has to be intentional. I mean, you were involved in the cross-examination or in the examination of the witness when that was exposed as completely untrue, yet it winds up back in their brief. That can't happen with 11 people checking it, unless it's intentional, I don't think. So that would be my response. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The situation -- this is not the first time that I have found myself faced with a similar situation. The only difference in the other cases when this happened - not here, I'm not referring to the Tribunal, I'm referring to my jurisdiction - was that obviously there you have the luxury of time which we don't have here. The situation as I see it is as follows: There are several points that you raise in that motion that are undoubtedly valid, and I see also -- I recognise from the Prosecution side they do recognise that some mistakes have actually occurred. However, the sanction that you are asking is practically the most serious sanction that one could contemplate, and therefore one has to deal with the motion at that level because what you're asking essentially is to declare the final brief null and void for all intents and purposes of law, strike it out of the records because of the mistakes that there are and references to Stakic, plus other submissions that they have made. At this point in time, our decision is as follows: We will be going through the whole process in detail, in greater detail amongst ourselves, Judge Janu, Judge Taya, and myself, but without prejudice to the motion that you have filed and to any further submission that is we might even call upon you to make in due course, we have decided that we will proceed first with the closing arguments. That's without prejudice, of course. And then we will allot -- we'll either come back to you to ask you whether you want to make further submissions, in which case we'll hear them, and then we will decide the motion. Or if there are no further submissions on your part to be made on that motion, then obviously we will decide it as we go along. In other words, it may well be that we could come back with a final decision on that motion as we are proceeding with the closing arguments, or we could leave it till the very end. But all the closing arguments that we are going to hear are going to be heard without prejudice to that motion and the decision that we might take. If we come to the conclusion that your motion deserves to be accepted, then obviously, I mean, we have to provide Ms. Korner, Prosecution, the proper remedy, and that will be a laborious exercise, but we will strike from our minds and from practically the records the closing arguments that we will be proceeding with. But that stands to be seen because it all depends on the decision we will be taking later on on the motion. In other words, Ms. Korner, you proceed with the closing arguments, and Mr. Ackerman proceeds with the closing arguments as if the motion did not exist for the time being. Then obviously, if we decide in favour of Mr. Ackerman's motion, then obviously we are going to give you the remedy because, of course, as you said, you will be basing your closing arguments basically on what you have in the final brief. But again, there is another matter because the final brief does not consist entirely and exclusively of the mistakes that... So let's put it like this. There are a lot of arguments that need to be addressed when it comes to your motion, and we will address them in due course. But this is the first time we are meeting today after you filed the motion. We have not had time to go into any depth in it. We have, of course, read it. We will wait for the Prosecution's response, and we will take it up from there. But if you need time to make submissions on the time and on the response, obviously we will give you all the opportunities. But first, we proceed with the closing arguments even though legally speaking and logically, we should have started with the motion. But forget it, because we don't have the luxury of doing that first without wasting the precious time that we have allocated for this case this week. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only suggestion I was going to make is that originally these arguments were scheduled to start on the Tuesday. If they started on the Tuesday instead of today, that would give Your Honours today because we can file our response within the next hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can file your response within the next hour just the same. I mean, I suppose someone is -- it's not being drafted now. I suppose --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It needs some corrections. Your Honour, I should point out I'm not going to go into the detail because I think this sort of low level tit-for-tat argument -- Your Honour, we can make the same points about the Defence brief, and we have done a couple of examples. Your Honour, we don't suggest that they did this deliberately. Your Honour, in that case, if Your Honours are of the view that the speeches should go ahead today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I believe we should do. Again, I mean, it's -- everything is open. But I suggest we don't waste a day, even if using the word "waste" -- "waste" is maybe not the correct way of describing it. I think we should still proceed and not lose time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one other matter before I can give my closing address, and that relates to what will be part of my closing address. Your Honour will recall that reasonably early on in this case, the allegation was made and as we suggested throughout the case, without any basis in any factual matters or any possible instructions that come about this, that any documents which formed part of the Prosecution's exhibits which had been provided by the agency then known as AID, now known as FOS, were forged, that no reliance could be placed on them altogether. Your Honour, that is now an argument that reappears in the Defence final brief, but the argument is still maintained that documents -- sorry, Your Honour, I'm just going to get the Defence final brief. That Your Honours should disregard -- yes, "Documents for which there is no evidence of authorship or authenticity are unreliable, and no weight should be attached to them." Your Honour, that's at page 2 of the Defence final brief. Your Honour, we attempted to do an exercise which -- to deal with that very point, and we decided to concentrate on the documents received from AID because although there's no specific mention of that in the final brief, nonetheless it's there. Your Honours have heard the countless times that this was brought up and the discussions there were. To go through the AID exhibits and identify where there was evidence from witness testimony which in some way corroborated or authenticated those documents, we couldn't obviously do the same exercise with every single, as it were, document where you can't see a stamp or a signature. Your Honour, I would be perfectly entitled to read through every single document identifying the pages and the witnesses who in some way, we would suggest, corroborated or authenticated a document as part of my closing address. It would, however, be a very long and tedious process, and it would certainly extend the length of my closing address by at least two hours. And I have well in mind Your Honours admonition to me in this case when I was attempting to read documents, and Mr. Ackerman's point that everybody could read. Your Honour, accordingly, we put it into a schedule. It runs to 243 pages because, and particularly in the light of the allegations that are made, we actually didn't just give the cite. We actually set it out, cut and paste from the transcripts the cites that we say supported the authenticity of the documents. Your Honour, I sent that document to Mr. Ackerman on Friday, and said that my application would be, rather than reading it out to Your Honours, which I am perfectly entitled to do, I would prefer to simply hand it in when I reach the appropriate point and deal with it that way so that Your Honours can see it. Your Honour, a reduced version of the schedule without actually showing verbatim what the evidence is runs to 12 pages. Your Honour, the objection, I understand it, is that this is a way to get round the page limitation of the pre-trial brief. Your Honour, first of all, it wasn't actually completed because the 11 people who in one form or another helped out in this brief, even that wasn't sufficient to get this document ready in time. The second thing, I would have been, had I wanted to, had I thought it was a proper document to put in with a pre-trial brief, I would have been able to because the practice direction allows one to put in annexes and schedules which run to -- Your Honour, I'm looking at the practice direction dated the 5th of March 2002. An appendix that would be a reasonably length, which is normally three times the page limit for that class of motion or brief. Your Honour, the page limit we were given was 300 pages. We could have up to 900 pages of annexes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, you don't need to proceed on this much further because the position I will explain it very clearly. This is not a simple case that could be dealt with with a few pages. I'm being very blunt. If you had asked, both of you or either of you, for more pages, we would certainly not have found difficulty because this is a case that needs examination. And it deserves...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I say, there are two options. I would be perfectly entitled, because it's an issue that has been raised in this case and is maintained, although apparently not in respect of the AID documents, that Your Honours having admitted these documents should give them no reliance unless we can show corroborating evidence. Your Honour, I say I could read this. I would prefer, as I've no doubt Your Honours would, simply to hand in the document, which Mr. Ackerman has had the opportunity to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's your position on this, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, not only did you impose page limits, but you also imposed time limits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This document was sent to me by email Friday afternoon around 3.00, as I recall. 243 pages of material that I have had absolutely no chance to even look at, let alone have a chance to fairly respond to. I think it's extraordinarily unfair to, at the last minute, produce that document when it has been clear from the pre-trial hearings in this case that we were contesting any document that didn't have a signature or a stamp, that didn't have some guarantees of trustworthiness and authenticity, to say at the last minute, "We noticed in the brief that we're still making that claim and therefore we have the right to file a 243-page addendum to our brief." This is not an addendum. This is material that should have been in the original brief. That's where it belongs. And that's what it is. Now, I understand, Your Honour, that this is an extraordinarily complex case, and it's a case that requires a great deal more than the ordinary case. You understand that, and I understand that, and the Prosecution understands that. But the Registry doesn't. The Registry doesn't understand that. The Registry limited us to 30 hours each per week for the time we could spend on this brief. We just recently got them to add some hours, but that's after the fact. The Prosecution was able to put 11 people to work on this brief. That's why they could do the full 300 pages plus all these annexes. We couldn't possibly do anything like that. We did not have the people or the hours to do any work -- to give this any justice at all. We could have easily filed a 300 page brief if we'd had time. We wrote the best brief we could, the two of us working unbelievable hours to get it done with the same time the Registry telling us they would only pay us for 30 hours a week because this wasn't a complex matter, this wasn't something that was unforeseen, and this wasn't something that required this much effort. So that's the situation we found ourselves in. We are now in a huge disadvantage to the Office of the Prosecutor because they can do things like this 243-page document they want to hand you today. They do have the staff to do those kinds of things. Now, how can there possibly be a fair trial when one side has so much greater resources to devote to the matter than the other side does. If we had the kind of resources the Prosecutor has, and they were limited like we were, they would be complaining bitterly that there's a total unfairness here, and they should be. Because there is. And so I think, not because this is a complex matter, not because it might be nice to have, but because it's totally unfair, you should not permit the Prosecutor to submit this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Roberts --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think Mr. Ackerman's grasped the point. First of all, can I deal with the 11 people. As I have said before over and over again, it is not the full-time application of everyone who works on this case to this case alone. We borrowed people to do various bits, and we thought it only right that they should get credit for helping us. Having said all that, I accept entirely that we've had more assistance than Mr. Ackerman has. But that's not the point. The point that I'm making is not -- Mr. Ackerman can't stop me doing this. It's a perfectly proper part comment that would form part of my closing address. All that I am asking to do is rather than waste, and it will take me some time to go through it, the time doing it, Your Honours should be able to see it in document form. May I put it this way: Mr. Ackerman, as I say, and I'm going to say again, raised this issue without any, we say, foundation at all. And so that is why we have to deal with it. And the issues are raised, as Mr. Ackerman rightly says, and I'm going to deal with it straight away, it's the Prosecution's duty to negate them. The burden remains throughout on the Prosecution. So Your Honour, that's what I'm asking you to do. Mr. Ackerman simply says it's unfair because he hasn't got as many people. Your Honour, that's not a ground for objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's saying two things actually. He's saying what you just said, and also that, strictly speaking, you were under notice that these documents were being contested not now but from months and months, if not years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you should have addressed it in your final brief, and that document should have been part of the final brief and not subsequent to it. Again, I think we should not be -- point taken, Mr. Ackerman. But the issue now, this is why I had addressed Mr. Roberts, because the last time we met here before we adjourned, we did deal with the question of which documents still remained challenged -- still remain challenged. I wouldn't remember the date, Mr. Roberts, but perhaps two --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid I don't remember any discussion about that at all. The last time we met, we went through Mr. Ackerman's documents that he submitted and had -- heard submissions on that. But I don't recall it ever being - I may, of course, be wrong, probably am - that Mr. Ackerman identified any particular class of documents that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, what happened was this, Ms. Korner: You both tried to wind up on that issue by making sure that all the documents that you wanted to be in were actually in. And the question arose, I had one of my staff pointing out to me that there were still some documents that had been challenged and we wanted to know whether they were still challenged or not, and that there were still some documents which you weren't quite sure whether they had been tendered or not. So went through the matter very quickly, both with regard to some Prosecution documents and with regard to some Defence documents. And there was a short list of documents that remained definitely challenged. I want to -- these AID were not discussed during that sitting, not that I can remember, not that -- perhaps Mr. Roberts can dig up the sitting. I wouldn't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I don't remember more than that. But Mr. Ackerman, Ms. Korner, in fact I do recollect now that there was a formal objection by Mr. Ackerman with regard to the Bosanski Petrovac Municipality which we dealt with very briefly during that sitting, I think adjourning the decision basically, if I remember well. And another document that was prepared -- what was the other document, Mr. Roberts? That's ours, no? That's ours, with regard to the totality of the documents that had been tendered by you, that means the Prosecution, and also by Mr. Ackerman. And we asked questions on a few of them. But I suppose we are wasting time. Let's find the records of that particular sitting. I don't remember when it was, but it was either the last one or if not the last one, the penultimate one. And we see what we discussed, what we discussed then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue is a fairly simple one. Your Honours, as I say, I can do the exercise if I have to by reading out effectively what's on the schedule we prepared. The application is only that instead of having to do that, I can hand it to Your Honours. It's not an exhibit. It's a guide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that's all that I'm asking. Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the position is this: This document, we accept to have this document handed to us. Then obviously, Mr. Ackerman, take your time to go through it, and whatever submissions you may require to make, you think you need to make on that document, you will have all the opportunity later on. And we have of course taken notice of your complaint that first this should have been handed as part of the pre-trial -- not pre-trial, the final brief. And that secondly, and that secondly there is this disparity of resources between the Prosecution and the Defence. That's something that is not being submitted for the first time. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond in writing, then? Would that be an appropriate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you prefer to respond in writing, then that's one option. If you think it's less time-consuming or you prefer to respond orally, you will be given the opportunity as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think I'll have time to go through it before we conclude our arguments here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, there is one other matter that I wanted to make sure of before we proceed. Mr. Ackerman, following the Prosecution's final brief, you also filed a motion to strike Appendix C. To that motion, the Prosecution has filed a response. We've seen both. We are in a position to decide that motion. But before we do so, we wanted to make sure whether also in the light of what point been said today you have any further submissions? Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, we have nothing other than the motion. We stand on the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You, too, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That matter will be decided in due course. In the meantime, we have the appendices, and we will decide what to do with them along with the motion. So Ms. Korner, are you ready to start with your closing arguments?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am. Or we are, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we want to start what we have to say to you today by looking at what Your Honours may feel, having heard the evidence, was one of the seminal meetings of this case. And that was the so-called Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina held in Banja Luka on the 12th of May 1992. It was by any standard a meeting of great importance, importance in the history of the conflict which by then had already begun in Bosnia. By the end of that meeting, the goals of the Bosnian Serbs had been clearly set out by Karadzic. Further, the physical means by which those goals were to be achieved had been put in place, in particular with the establishment of the Bosnian Serb Army, the VRS. And really, for the first time, what the Prosecution say was this criminal plan of the Bosnian Serbs was exposed. All the major players, if I can use that expression, in the Bosnian Serb leadership were present, with the one exception of Biljana Plavsic who apparently sent her congratulations over the telephone during the course of this assembly in respect of the establishment of the VRS. There present were Karadzic, Krajisnik, Mladic, Talic, Ostojic, Kupresanin, and of course this accused, Radoslav Brdjanin. Some of the things that were said during the course of this assembly the Prosecution suggest were really important for the consideration which Your Honours will have to apply to the allegations made by the Prosecution. Karadzic, when he was outlining what has come to be known as "the six strategic goals of the Bosnian Serbs" said, and Your Honour all of these quotes are taken from the Exhibit P50: "The first goal is separation from the other two national communities, separation of states, separation from those who are our enemies and who have used every opportunity, especially in this century, to attack us and who would continue with such practices if we were to continue to stay together in the same state." In other words, one of the features, the Muslims, the Croats are our enemies, and they are the people who are going to attack us unless we act pre-emptively. That's one of the themes that was stressed throughout this period of time. Dragan Kalinic: "Have we chosen the option of war or the option of negotiation? I say this with a reason, and I must instantly add that knowing who our enemies are, how perfidious they are, how they cannot be trusted until they are physically, militarily destroyed and crushed, which of course implies eliminating and liquidating their key people." Your Honour, the Prosecution suggests that there in that single sentence is summed up the whole concept of the genocide that the Prosecution suggest occurred in Bosnia in the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Kalinic ended that part by saying: "I do not hesitate in selecting the first option, the option of war." Miroslav Vijestica from Krupa, a deputy to the assembly: "No more Muslims in the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa. Will they have a place to return to? I think it is unlikely, after our president told us the happy news that the right bank of the Una River was the border." That's a reference to the one of the strategic goals. And he went on to say: "As for Bosanski Novi, let me tell you that I was there yesterday." The 11th of May that would be. "Bosanski Novi is sealed off. An ultimatum has been issued, and a deadline set for the Muslims to surrender their weapons. Some of them have; some have not. Yesterday, there was shooting. What will happen today? I believe they will surrender. The same is going on in Sanski Most. I think that the Muslims will be disarmed there, too." Your Honour, again, there encapsulated of the Prosecution will be saying to you has been shown clearly from the evidence the disarmament leading to the violence against the Muslims and Croats. And finally, Radoslav Brdjanin: "I would like to say a heartfelt bravo to Mr. Kalinic. In all my appearances in this joint assembly, it has never crossed my mind that though he seems quiet, while I seem hawkish, that his opinions are the closest to mine. I believe that this is the formula, and we should adhere to this formula." The Defence suggest that by those words Brdjanin was referring to Kalinic's suggestion that the JNA weapons should be prevented from leaving Bosnia. Now, Your Honours, we invite the Trial Chamber to read both speeches in full and decide whether there is any merit in that suggestion. If so, then no doubt the Trial Chamber will not for one moment rely on this speech as evidence which is adverse to Mr. Brdjanin. But we suggest that common sense, and looking at those speeches, it can refer to nothing else but Kalinic's -- the part of Kalinic's speech which said that their enemies should be physically, militarily destroyed and crushed. Your Honours, so in effect, this assembly brought together the major themes which have occupied so much time in this case. The overall plan of the leadership, a description of how it was already being put into effect in various areas, its military component, and most importantly, we would say, a snapshot of the role and the intent that Mr. Brdjanin played and held throughout this period. Your Honours, it's a long time since we've looked at the video of that assembly, and I'm going to ask that it is now -- Your Honours are briefly reminded of the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I think that's all we needed of that video. Your Honour, can I make it absolutely clear in the light of the beginning of the Defence final brief that this is a prosecution of an individual, Radoslav Brdjanin, not a people, "the Serbs," the Bosnian Serbs or the Serb Serbs, any more than the prosecution of Kordic and Cerkez were a prosecution of the whole of the Bosnian Croats, or the prosecution of Hadzihasanovic and Kubura are a prosecution of the Bosniaks as a people. Radoslav Brdjanin has been prosecuted because we allege and say now that there is clear and unambiguous evidence that he committed the offences with which he has been charged. The Prosecution does not challenge, which is the word used in the Defence final brief, this Trial Chamber to decide this case upon the law and the facts; it is in no doubt having been in front of Your Honours for the past two years plus that this Trial Chamber will do just that, as it would do whatever the nationality or ethnicity, whichever is the proper word, of the accused. And the Prosecution equally has no doubt that the Trial Chamber will only convict if it finds that it is satisfied so that it is sure on all the evidence on both the Prosecution and the Defence that the accused is guilty of all or any of those charges, satisfied, so sure being the same thing as beyond a reasonable doubt. If it is not so satisfied, then clearly it will acquit. And we have no doubt that in neither case will it be swayed by sympathy, nor by the media, nor by the international community who have not heard all the evidence on a daily basis in the same way as Your Honours. Your Honours, we have no doubt, will bring a professional, objective view to bear on the evidence in this case. We accept, we embrace the fact that the burden and the standard of proof remains throughout on the Prosecution to satisfy you so that you are sure that Brdjanin is guilty of all or any of these offences. We emphasise, as I already raised this morning, that no burden rests upon Radoslav Brdjanin to prove his innocence. We have the burden to discharge both in terms of the evidence that we bring and to nullify any evidence which the defendant may have brought on his behalf in support of his case. But, Your Honour, we do say this: If facts are introduced into evidence through witness testimony or documents which are not disputed through other evidence, and I emphasise "through other evidence," then the Trial Chamber is entitled to say, "We find that fact proved." For example, that Radoslav Brdjanin did make a speech saying that only 2 or 3 per cent of Muslims would be allowed to remain in Banja Luka. Or as another example, more than 200 people were murdered by the police at Mount Vlasic, about which I'll have more to say later on in my address. And I say that, Your Honour, because there has been no evidence to contradict either of those facts which we put before you by way of evidence. Now, Your Honour, there have been lengthy, written submissions from both sides detailing the evidence in support of the submissions of law and of fact. And subject to the caveat that we dealt with earlier this morning, this address that we are making to you today and tomorrow is not going to rehearse everything that has already been said. Instead, we propose to attempt to deal with what appear to be the major issues in this case and to remind the Trial Chamber orally and visually of some of the reality of the more cogent evidence. Your Honours, I hope you will forgive me if I'm, to use the English expression, teaching my grandmother to suck eggs, if I digress for a moment or so on the question of what is evidence. What is evidence? It's the testimony of witnesses and the contents of documents admitted as exhibits, and of course any agreed facts. Your Honour, I think it's important to emphasise that for the other extreme of what is not evidence. Suggestions made by counsel to witnesses that things happened or were said or vice versa, that things did not happen or were not said, and those suggestions made to a witness are denied by the witness, and I'll come to a couple of examples in a moment, well unless there is evidence which supports those assertions, those suggestions, they remain unsubstantiated suggestions, no more really than comment, putting it at its highest. And Your Honour, we will suggest should not be taken into consideration. Your Honour, can I give you some examples. The suggestion not even really made to a witness, but that documents which came from AID were forgeries; the suggestion made to witnesses that Mr. Brdjanin, because it was alleged that his two brothers were in mixed marriages, would never - and I think this is the way it was put - would never -- would neither have thought or uttered such words dealing with what should happen to children of mixed marriages, that was put to Witness BT-22. And the reaction was, "No, he said that." And indeed, you may think as a suggestion it has been completely nullified because even Mr. Radic agreed that that was one of his, if I can put it that way, better speeches. And I use that word sarcastically. Your Honour, the speech about, and I've already dealt with, the percentage of non-Serbs who would be allowed to remain in Banja Luka, the suggestion was put to a number of witnesses that that speech was never made by Mr. Brdjanin, again, Your Honour, no evidence to suggest to the contrary, just a suggestion by counsel. Your Honour, Mr. Ackerman in the course of dealing with the Celinac documents got up and said that they did not agree that Mr. Brdjanin became a member of the Celinac Crisis Staff. Well, Your Honour, whether they agreed or not, the clear and we suggest undisputed evidence on the face of the document that we produced is that P, and I give the number of that document, P1993, shows that he was a member of the Celinac Municipal Crisis Staff. Now, Your Honours, some of the evidence which relates, for example, to the existence of an overall plan or to the authority wielded by Radoslav Brdjanin is circumstantial. It requires inferences to be drawn. And one of the reasons for that is that there are vital records and documents missing, notwithstanding the number of exhibits that exist in this case. For example, the ARK Crisis Staff minutes of meetings, which is a topic that I'm going to return to; the minutes of the Municipal Crisis Staff in Celinac; in Teslic; in Prijedor; in Bosanski Novi; in Bosanska Krupa, all of those records are mysteriously missing, disappeared, flooded, whatever the various explanations were. Your Honour, of course, the other aspect is, and this was very clearly enunciated by Witness BT-94, that you couldn't hear anyone say, "let's go and kill everyone in the village," "let's raze Srebrenica to the ground," "let's destroy them," there was no such thing. In other words, no one in the leadership, including Radoslav Brdjanin, said in terms: "Our plan encompasses the persecution, the destruction, in whole or in part, of the Muslim and Croat populations within the territory of Republika Srpska," as it now is. And I'm going to refer to it, although it had a slightly different name in that period. Although, as we have submitted to you, they came very close to that, but there was never that clear enunciation of that criminal intent. But the fact that evidence may be circumstantial does not make it, we submit, any less compelling. It has been said that circumstantial evidence is often the best evidence; it is evidence of surrounding circumstances which by undesigned coincidence is capable of proving a proposition with the accuracy of mathematics, and it is no derogation of evidence to say that it is circumstantial, and I see Your Honour nodding. And I imagine Your Honour is familiar with the case from which it is taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have quoted it in several of my judgements, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we submit that if you look at the evidence of the circumstances, the repetition of the same type of events in the different municipalities which we will come to, the documents which reveal what the Municipal Crisis Staffs were deciding upon and discussing, then the inferences are, we submit, irresistible. And in particular, that there was a plan which involved the commission of these offences, and that the accused, Radoslav Brdjanin, played an active part in that plan and its implementation. Your Honour, can I come to the question, and I'm just dealing very generally with some matters at the moment, of witnesses. Your Honour, the Prosecution called 120 live, that is to say, viva voce, in-this-court witnesses, some were called in full, others who had already testified or made statements were brought for cross-examination effectively. The remaining witnesses, some 82, were tendered under the provisions of Rule 92 bis. In other words, their evidence, it was accepted they were not required to attend for cross-examination. Your Honour, there were some seven witnesses who I will call very loosely international witnesses. There were 13 witnesses of Serb nationality called by the Prosecution and 3 experts. The remaining witnesses were those who were victims of or witnesses to crimes. Your Honour, in any trial, it is axiomatic that the finders of fact have to make an assessment, not just of what was said by the witness, but of the witness himself. The internal question I suppose that one asks is was that witness honest, truthful, and accurate? Because however long ago the events, they were clearly engraved on his memory, and he or she will never forget them. The second category, was the witness honest, but in this case because of the length of time and the nature of the events that the witness has to describe, possibly inaccurate on some matters, for example, dates, the exact sequence of events, identification of persons responsible. But nonetheless, still essentially reliable on the major events described. And a third category, is the witness's evidence so confused that it would be unfair to place any reliance on it? And it's right to say that there have been probably been one of every category called. At the other extreme, there are the witnesses who in some part or other of their evidence have deliberately lied to the Court in order to try and mislead. There are some witnesses who may have lied about everything; other witnesses who told the truth on some matters but lied about others. Your Honour, this is, we would submit, particularly relevant when looking at the Serb witnesses who were called both by the Prosecution and by the Defence. The Defence in their final brief advised the Trial Chamber to be careful because of partisan distortion. That was the phrase used. And we agree. It has a possible application to all witnesses who were involved in the events in the Autonomous Region of Krajina in 1991 and 1992. But if it applies to all, we would say it applies particularly to those who were associates to a greater or lesser degree of Radoslav Brdjanin because they clearly wished to present those events to which they were a party in a light the most favourable to them. And they wished to present their own participation in those events in as favourable a light as possible and in a way which takes them as far as away from the centre of the action as it is possible to be. And Your Honour, for such witnesses, the Trial Chamber may have to, probably will, and indeed probably should look for evidence which supports or contradicts aspects of their testimony which the Trial Chamber considers to be important. For example, if they made previous statements in interview or in the media or elsewhere; documents which came into existence at the time; the evidence of other witnesses dealing with those events and those documents. But Your Honour, even if there is no such supporting evidence, such corroborating evidence, you, the Judges, the professional Judges, will no doubt and should make a judgement and decide which parts of the evidence you accept and which parts you reject. Now, Your Honour, the witnesses called by the Defence, and of course the Defence don't have to call any witnesses at all. They are perfectly entitled to sit back and say, "The Prosecution has the burden of proof. We're calling no evidence." But in this case, they chose to call witnesses. Your Honour may have thought in listening to those witnesses that you may have been assisted perhaps from hearing more from other members of the crisis staff in the Autonomous Region of Krajina; for example, Mr. Kupresanin, Mr. Milanovic, those people who were not only members of the crisis staff, but in Kupresanin's case, was the original president of the assembly of the autonomous region, and there are some unanswered questions about some of those meetings which I'm going to come to. Also, a delegate to the Assembly of the Serbian People. Mr. Milanovic, who was not only a member - we'll have a look at the members of the crisis staff in a moment - of the crisis staff, but a vice-president of the government of the Republika Srpska. Colonel Vojinovic, who attended the meetings on behalf of General Talic, the commander for civilian affairs. Well, Your Honour, you didn't hear from them, and that is a matter, of course, that Your Honours may want to consider as to the reason why you didn't hear from them. Now, Your Honours, much of the compelling evidence in this case does, in fact, come from the documents. Your Honours, the challenge to the documents as I've already referred to provided by AID came fairly early on in the trial, around the 15th of May when it was asserted by Mr. Ackerman that, "Documents which come from the AID office in Bihac I think is a very suspicious source of documents to start with. I think there's at least the possibility that it's just a pure forgery." And then with the arrest of the AID officials later on during the trial, then the challenges were brought forward again, arrest which had nothing to do with any of the period or the events that this trial is concerned with. Your Honour, as we said, we can't carry out this exercise on every single, unsigned, unstamped document. So we've taken a particular class of documents. But Your Honours, I have no doubt, with the assistance of your legal officers, will be able to look at the other unsigned documents and carry out probably the same exercise. So Your Honour, what we have done, we have reduced into schedule form, and can I ask that it be handed to Your Honours now. Your Honour, would you -- there are two -- there's one that contains all the actual words, there's a shorter version which simply gives the references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have already discussed this, Ms. Korner. We require both. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, they will be handed up to you, then. Your Honour will see, as I say, this is not meant to be an exhibit. This is no more than a guide. Effectively, this is the comment we make. We say there is evidence to show that these are documents. But Your Honour, Your Honours will see it's confidential because it refers to a number of closed session testimony and the like. So if it's going to go to the Registry, it should be marked under seal, but it's not an exhibit. Now, Your Honour, as we've dealt with this morning also, there's no repetition of this allegation in the Defence final brief, and I would like to take it from that. And I'm going to come to some other issues that are not dealt with that this is not being pursued, but every time I've taken that view I have been sadly deceived. I have been told, no, that all issues are still live issues. Now, Your Honour, we say that if they're saying that time and the expense was -- if one carried out the exercise with the other unsigned documents, one would probably be able...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, lest there be some misunderstanding, if I heard properly, I'm being asked to say whether I still object to the documents that I have objected to on the record in this case, or am I withdrawing those objections because I didn't say anything in my final brief. I'm not withdrawing any objections to documents. They all stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, quite. It's what I sadly anticipated would be the case. But Your Honour, as I say, we would submit that if the exercise we carried out with these particular class of documents were carried out with others, there is existing in the record of this case ample evidence to show that in particular the important documents are confirmed, corroborated in some form or other by witness testimony, and indeed other documents. Your Honour, can I deal, for example, with another class of documents, and those are what we have been calling the Milos documents. The reports submitted to the DSB in Banja Luka, CSB, DSB, to Mr. Kesic. Your Honours, they were strongly objected to in the beginning of the case on the basis that nobody knew who Milos was, nobody knew what it was about. Your Honour, I'm not going to quote the evidence because this is the Defence evidence in closed session, but the evidence of BW-1 you may have thought laid this to rest. May I give you the page reference, and I hope it's the correct one. It's transcript 1836 to 45. No, I'm sorry -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, no. Your Honour, I'm sorry. That is the wrong reference because this is what was said on behalf, in fact, at the time of General Talic about the Milos documents, that there is a whole series of documents signed by a certain individual by the name of Milos whose identity we do not know. This person is not identifiable, and we consider these documents to be anonymous documents. This Chamber decided on the 5th of February this year not to admit a document because it was an anonymous document and because the Defence could not proceed with the verification of the authenticity and the credibility of the documents. We believe that the documents signed by this individual by the name of Milos fall exactly in the same category. Your Honour, that was said on the 18th of February at transcript page 1836 to 45, and the evidence of BW-1, Your Honours, I haven't, unfortunately I don't think got the transcript reference. But I can provide that after the break. Your Honour, any documents without a stamp or a signature were objected to globally as well. Your Honours, Mr. Radojko, and I'm going to have a little bit to say about him later on, when he was shown the exhibit P1814, which was an unsigned, unstamped Petrovac document, said this: "There is no signature. And I think not because it is a filed copy." Your Honour, earlier witnesses said some of the filed copies didn't get signed. "Because according to our administrative rules, it should have been signed, too. That copy should have been signed, too, but I think that this was done by the then-SDS secretary who had a law education, but he wasn't very tidy, and presumably that is why the signature is lacking. I now recall that at that time, that is late 1991, Stevo Radosevic was the president of the SDS rather than Ivanic. Radosevic left that office I think because he was a private businessman and this particular duty interfered with his business. But I still think this is an authentic document." Your Honour, I thought I had given references for everything, but I'll have to check that one over the break as well, the page number. Your Honour, the other aspect of this case that Your Honours may find slightly extraordinary is that the Defence apparently adopted a schizoid attitude towards these unsigned, unstamped, forged documents. Some of them they were using themselves to make points. The real explanation is not schizoid at all. Those that help them are okay, not objected to, Your Honour should take them into account. Those that hurt them are objectionable. Your Honours, again, we say using your own knowledge and experience and looking at the other evidence you've heard, you will decide what weight to attach, and we would suggest disregard the blanket prohibition which is suggested in the Defence final brief that any document unsigned and unstamped -- I'm sorry, that documents for which no evidence of authorship, for which there is no evidence of authorship are unreliable and no weight should be attached to them. Your Honour, that, then, would be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I, just before I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because Mr. Brdjanin is not yet in his place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- continue my address, raise matters really affecting the law. First of all, Your Honour, obviously at this moment the judgement is being given in Krstic. If there's any major change in the law, then I think it'll will have to be in writing because we'll need to consider the judgement, as will both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Same here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Your Honour, the other matter that occurs to me is, Your Honour, we've answered all Your Honours' questions in writing. However, if Your Honours tomorrow when I've completed my remarks on the facts would wish me to address any further matters, it will be exceedingly helpful if Your Honours could let me know by the end of today simply because otherwise I'm going to be answering off the top of my head, whereas if I have some advance notice then I can prepare any replies overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know if Your Honours will have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know either. I will discuss it with Judge Janu and Judge Taya and Mr. Roberts later on. But at the present moment, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's most helpful, Your Honour. Can I just give Your Honours the reference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is reference --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- The reference first of all to evidence given by BW-1 where he dealt with Milos, that's at transcript page number 23364 to 23365.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's where he identified Milos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's where he identified him, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the part of Radojko's evidence that I read to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The P1814?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P1814 is at transcript page number 20036 to 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, can I now come to the topic of the missing documents which I referred to a little earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The ARK Crisis Staff meetings, the minutes thereof, according to Mr. Blagojevic, none were ever taken. He was asked at transcript page 21727, this was in chief, "specifically, were you ever tasked, were you ever asked to be responsible for the taking of minutes or anything like that?" And he said: "No. I was never responsible for the minutes." That was picked up in cross-examination -- no, I'm sorry, it was still examination-in-chief, I'm sorry. And it was put to him, I believe it was Mr. Cunningham, "I know you didn't take the minutes. You've told us that. I'm wondering if you wrote down anything during these meetings. If you did so, whether there's any of those documents still in existence today." And he said: "No, no. Under the item `draft conclusion' which would take up one page, we would write our suggestions." There were other bits and pieces, but those were the major parts. And that was said at T21729. It was then picked up in cross-examination. This was dealing with the very early part where he had been seen back in 1996, I believe it was, by investigators with the Office of the Prosecution, and he had had that meeting. And this was put to him: "I want to ask you this, Mr. Blagojevic. Was what was in that folder" - you remember the folder that disappeared as well - "which you refused to let the representatives see, did that contain the minutes of the meetings of the crisis staff of the region?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's because according to you, no minutes were ever taken. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's right. That's at page 21808. And then later on: "Who told you" - this is the question - "that you need not take minutes?" Answer: "Well, quite simply, it was impossible to take minutes." And he gave a very long explanation about the nature of the meetings. And that's at 21889. Now, Your Honour, that was clearly a lie. It was demonstrated to be a lie by the evidence of the very next witness, Mr. Radic. Question, and this was in cross-examination: "Do you agree that you told us in Banja Luka in July 2001 that not only was Mr. Blagojevic taking minutes, but that you noticed one day he was making a mistake in them?" Answer: "Yes, that is what I stated here, that he did not reflect what I said regarding the replacement of the Banja Luka University dean." That's at page 22074. And later: "Can we put it this way, Mr. Radic: It is inconceivable to you, is it not, that a record of a body such as the regional crisis staff or any crisis staff did not have somebody noting down what was being discussed?" Answer: "That's how it should be, that one had to know who was the president, who was the secretary, and what the official minutes were." And that was on the same page, 22074. And finally, to show that the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies to you, Ms. Korner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, finally, as I say, to show that the Defence themselves didn't believe the witness they had called, was this. This was again to Mr. Radic from whoever counsel was, and I can't now recall. "I just want to ask you this: When you go back to Banja Luka, if you have any ability whatsoever to find the minutes from the ARK Crisis Staff, if you can find anyone who has them, if you can encourage anyone to locate them, we would desperately like to have them. So can you please try to do that. And with that, that's all I have. Thank you." In fact, I can see from my own note it was Mr. Ackerman, because Your Honours said "I thank you, Mr. Ackerman." And the witness then said: "Was that a question, Mr. Ackerman?" And a very good point that was, too. "Or the secretary who had already testified here, Mr. Blagojevic, should have those minutes. I really don't have them. I don't know where they were kept or whether there were any in the first place." And then this remarkably: "I must tell you that I really doubt whether these minutes ever existed. There were not that many meetings in the first place, and I sincerely doubt that any written documents were kept." And that is at T22343, transcript, I should say. Now, Your Honour, it's not as I say just the ARK Crisis Staff minutes and other documents which are missing, but the minutes from the crisis staffs in other municipalities. Those in particular which remained throughout as part of the Republika Srpska and were never entered by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1995, for example, as I said, Celinac, Teslic, and Prijedor. All of these mysteriously vanished before the searches were carried out in Prijedor, as Your Honours know, in 1997, and in Banja Luka in 1998. The Assembly documents by and large are available. Of course, most of the assemblies were not meeting during the highly relevant period, except on the odd occasion. Your Honours, we suggest that those documents are missing because the people responsible for keeping them or still in charge in these municipalities know full well that they would provide clear evidence of the municipal crisis staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object pretty strongly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection upheld. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to interrupt you in the least, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the first thing I was going to say. It's normal courtesy in my jurisdiction not to interrupt a final speech and to save any objections that you may have to content until the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the second matter is this: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, please try to stick -- I mean, I was explaining to Judge Janu and Judge Taya how important it is that we don't to interrupt you whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will accept what is standard in Ms. Korner's jurisdiction and not interrupt any further. If I have anything to say, I'll say it at the end. I think that's a sensible suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I am also making points here, marks of what I will refer back to you arising from Ms. Korner. So let's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say this: I am entitled to make suggestions to Your Honour which are inferences which can be drawn from evidence which is in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We suggest those are proper inferences to draw because if one looks at the minutes that we do have, those from Kotor Varos, for example, from Sanski Most, and from Kljuc, they do, we suggest, show clear involvement of the crisis staff in those crimes. And therefore, the fact that with searches and requests we have never, ever been able to recover the other crisis staff minutes, it is a proper inference to Your Honours to draw. Your Honour, it is as a result of those missing documents that the schedule or the two schedules of the implementation of the crisis staff decisions are necessarily constrained because we only have a limited selection, some four or five municipalities out of the 13 that we have called evidence where we have the relevant and appropriate documents. Now, Your Honours, the next question I want to deal with is one again that we have touched on earlier today, and that was some of the issues raised in the case which I was going to say seemed to have been abandoned in the sense that they're not mentioned at all in the Defence final brief. But I have no doubt at all, and to save Mr. Ackerman getting up to say it, that he will say all these issues are still maintained. Your Honour, the first was an issue that was at some stage raised, that there never was an overall plan by the Bosnian Serb leadership which involved the commission of criminal offences. Your Honour, that is not in any way maintained in the Defence final brief. What is said is that Mr. Brdjanin was not a party to any such plan. Secondly, Your Honour, the variant A and B document, one of the major issues in the case was and certainly at an early stage, that it was either never issued by the SDS or alternatively, if issued, never distributed. And the importance of this document is clear. It's demonstrated by the fact that in every case other than the first case, that of Tadic, in every case that has involved the prosecution of a Bosnian Serb, there was a dispute about this document. And Your Honours, it led to the SDS in 2001 when they were asked for the original version of this document by this Office issuing a denial that this document was ever produced or issued by them. Your Honours, I think you now see it on the screen. Your Honours, it is Exhibit DB46. Your Honours, it's dated you will see the 5th of November 2001. Subject: Reply to your memo. And that was the request for various documents, original documents, from the SDS archives. And Your Honour, the relevant part of the letter is on the second page of the document. "The main board as well as any other SDS body never considered or instructed the organisation and activation of Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina at its sessions. We were informed that such instructions were given by a certain number of retired officers of the former Yugoslav People's Army." And it's signed, "Head of the SDS main office, Milovan Bjelica." Now, Your Honour, it is, we would submit to Your Honours, clear evidence of how important this document is considered to be that even in 2001, the SDS, flying in the face of all the evidence that not only Your Honours but other Trial Chambers have heard about this document, should persist in this denial that this document was issued by them. And although a valiant rear-guard action has been put up by the Defence to maintain this denial, even after one of their own witnesses said that he had received it, we would submit it does seem as though that is now abandoned. That's not surprising because in fact, I said their own witness. There were two Defence witnesses who both testified that they had received the document in their municipalities. The first was Radic in Banja Luka, and that one can see at page 22167. And the second was Kalabic, the assemblyman, the delegate, the deputy from Kljuc, and that can be seen at T22576. And it is submitted that the clear and unambiguous evidence that this document was issued by the Main Board of the SDS and received by the municipal boards includes, and we didn't include every example, all these documents have been entered into evidence, the Kljuc Crisis Staff, Zvornik, which is not in the area because it's discussed on the 23rd of December; same date discussed by Bratunac, again, that's not in the area but we put the exhibit in; 24th of December, Bosanska Krupa; 26th of December, Bosanski Petrovac; 27th of December, discussed by Prijedor SDS board; discussed the same day in a municipality outside the Autonomous Region of Krajina, Trnovo; 3rd of January in another municipality, Ilidza, the assembly there; and on the 15th of January, it was discussed by the Sanski Most municipal board. On the 26th of January 1992 at the session of the Assembly of the Serbian People, the coordinator, as he was described or appointed, of the governments of the autonomous regions, Mr. Cizmovic, called for the implementation of the second phase of the 19th of December instructions. On the 14th of February, 1992, it was discussed by the SDS Main Board, the Executive Board, and deputies at a meeting held in the Holiday Inn Sarajevo. There Karadzic stated that what was then called the second degree of the variant A and B instructions documents should be implemented. And later, the instructions were discussed by the following municipalities, 15th of February Donji Vakuf crisis staff; 17th of February Prijedor SDS municipal board, who were implementing the second stage; 3rd of March in Tuzla. And according to witness testimony, the instructions were received in Teslic and implemented. And finally, Your Honours, should there be any doubt, it was published in full in March 1992 by the Slobodna Bosna newspaper. Your Honour, the increasingly desperate attempts, not just in this Trial Chamber, as I say, but in others, to deny the provenance of this document and its distribution, we submit can only be because it is recognised for what it is, and that is a basic - and I say, I emphasise basic - blueprint for the illegal actions which were taken to seize control of the municipalities by force where necessary. So Your Honour, I hope that we have laid to rest through evidence any doubt that Your Honours may have ever entertained that the variant A and B document existed and was distributed. And as we say, the only reason that the various Bosnian Serbs persist in this denial is because they recognise it for what it is. Your Honour, other issues which were not mentioned in the final brief by the Defence was the SOS. However, that was revived again in the reply to our brief where what we suggest was an exceedingly lame attempt in the light of the evidence, it was made to suggest that the SOS were, and I quote, "Exactly what the SOS leaders say they were, disgruntled soldiers." That's at page 2, footnote 3. Your Honour, I'm going to turn to the topic of the SOS later. Your Honour, I've already dealt with the AID forgers. Your Honour, in the Defence final brief, there is nothing about Muslim resistance. Again, Your Honours, we say that's not surprising when the reality of such resistance as there was, what it actually amounted to is clear from the evidence, and again I'm going to turn to that. No suggestion is made in the Defence final brief that the crimes were committed by "out of control paramilitaries." I quote that from various suggestions made in the course of the evidence. That suggestion, of course, runs counter to the evidence of who was, in fact, responsible for the major crimes, which is the police and the military forces. And finally, the suggestion that the order to disarm applied to Serb paramilitaries as well as - and possibly even more so at one stage was the suggestion and - not merely to non-Serbs who possessed weapons. That is not repeated in the Defence final brief, and again that, we say, is a suggestion that in the light of all the evidence Your Honours heard, not only from the Muslim and Croats who gave evidence, but also from the Serbs, that clearly whatever the order may not say, it was an order directed entirely against the Muslim and Croat population. Your Honour, these are just some of the issues which the Defence raised during the trial which it has not raised or had not raised again in its final brief, and Your Honour which we on behalf of the Prosecution submit that we are clearly, in accordance with our burden, proved were suggestions without any merit. Your Honour, that concludes what I have to say in general terms about some of the aspects of this case. I now want to move to the criminal plan, the overarching or overall criminal plan as it's sometimes described. Whilst as we've already stated there seems to be no further challenge to the evidence that there was such a criminal plan, nonetheless it's important we feel to emphasise some of that evidence. Your Honours, the evidence is set out in full in Section 2A of our final brief. But Your Honour, can I say and remind Your Honours that effectively Karadzic made it clear in public and even more so in private what awaited the Muslims and Croats of Bosnia if they pursued the path of seeking independence. And can I invite Your Honours now to look, please, at Exhibit 2383.8, which is one of the intercepts. It was a conversation held on the 12th of October between someone called Rajko Djogo and Karadzic. Your Honour, can I ask Your Honours first of all to look at page 2 of the document. And if we can highlight about two-thirds of the way down the page, this is talking about the assembly. It was attended, Izetbegovic speaking. And then "gentlemen, we will not, and you can let them do whatever you want. We let them, but they are preparing for war. They will try to wage war here." And Mr. Djogo says "they will?" And

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC SAYS
utterances.text: "Probably as soon as next week." And again, we see this theme: We are only reacting to what the Muslims are preparing for us. Then at the bottom of the page, when Mr. Djogo sensibly says, "Well, what's he thinking to start a war in Sarajevo, is he crazy? Precisely." Answer by Mr. Karadzic: "He's, I think they -- exactly. They would be thrashed if they start a war. They will -- they'll disappear." That's the first time. And then if we go to the next page, at the top -- Your Honour, it's now turned into a highlighted.... "There will be rivers of blood," says Mr. Djogo. Second time within a matters of seconds: "They will disappear. That people will disappear from the face of the earth if they start now. Our offer was their only chance. Even that was too much, what we offered them." Your Honour, three times in the space of a few seconds "disappear." If we can go now, please, to the seventh page, and a very long answer by Mr. Karadzic -- Court I Sanction is obviously better for the Milosevic case. Your Honour will see there's a long answer by Karadzic down there. "They have to know that there are some 20.000 armed Serbs around Sarajevo. That's insane. They will disappear." Fourth time. "Sarajevo will be a black cauldron where 300.000 Muslims will die. They are not right in the head. I don't know. Now I will have to talk to them openly. "People, don't screw around. There are three, four hundred thousand armed Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. What are you thinking of? Plus there's the army and the hardware, and everything. Do you think you can secede just like Croatia?"" Secede. Thank you, Your Honour. And finally, Your Honour, on the next page, and the third section there, Karadzic again. Perhaps I will take it from the top. "We are not banning them from establishing," something or other. And Mr. Djogo says: "And then in the end, they will enter Banja Luka." Karadzic: "Yes, to Ozren, Doboj, anything he can rule, over half of Sarajevo. Zenica and half of Tuzla. And that's it, it's finished. Gracanica and the -- They don't understand that they will be up to their necks in blood, and that the Muslim people would disappear. The poor Muslims would disappear who don't know where he is taking them, where he is taking the Muslims." Your Honour, there cannot, we suggest, be any doubt of what Mr. Karadzic at that stage was threatening would happen because for the very obvious and logical reason that the Serbs in Bosnia had overwhelming firepower and military means. Now, Your Honour, on the intercepts, and this is a slight digression, but as I'm dealing for the first time with an intercept, the Defence made the point in their final brief that there was no wiretap as they call it on Brdjanin and say that indicates his lack of authority. That's at page 141 of the Defence brief at footnote 394. I'm sorry, and there is a footnote 394, and Your Honour, I said I wouldn't do it, but I can't resist it. That footnote which refers to a transcript at 18876 provides no authority for the assertion that he wasn't wiretapped because he wasn't important enough. Your Honour, in fact, as is clear from the evidence, the wiretaps were placed on telephones in Sarajevo. However, it does appear that Mr. Brdjanin himself believed that he was being intercepted or wiretapped because he told Mr. Karadzic in one of the conversations on the 13th of September of 1991 that his telephone was tapped. And that's P2382.7. That's the exhibit number. Now, Your Honours, can I ask you next to have a look, please, at Exhibit P2656.1. Well, I could ask Your Honours to have a look at it if the equipment was working, but I'm told that it's not. Your Honour, I'm just wondering if there's any chance we can move to Court I tomorrow where we know it works. I think the best thing is, Your Honour, if -- I don't know whether you have the exhibits there, if we can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what we will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, you can proceed so that we don't lose time. It's a long document, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, this is -- no, that's .2. Your Honours I'll identify it, and then I'll put my own copy on the ELMO. It's P2656.1, and it's Karadzic's speech of the 15th of October. I'm not going to play the video for Your Honours; this is the transcript. In fact, I think Your Honours have seen it very recently with Professor Shoup. Your Honours, this is part of the speech that Karadzic made. And he's saying this in respect of the potential negotiations: "I am asking you one more time. I am not threatening, but asking, to take seriously the interpretation of the political will of the Serbian people which is represented here by the Serbian Democratic Party and Serbian movement of renewal and several Serbs from some other parties. Please take it seriously. It is not good what you are doing. This is the road that you want Bosnia and Herzegovina to take, the same highway of hell and suffering that Slovenia and Croatia went through. Don't think you won't take Bosnia and Herzegovina to hell and the Muslim people in possible extinction because the Muslim people will not be able to defend itself if it comes to war here."
